setup: Zero-threshold two-way collateral agreement, margin period of risk 20 days. On one simulated path the portfolio is worth $-55$ (USD m) to the bank 20 days before the counterparty defaults and $-50$ at default. The bank's posted collateral tracks the value 20 days earlier, and on default none of it comes back.
ask: The bank's credit exposure at default is:

options.label: Zero: the portfolio is worth less than zero to the bank
options.why: Looked only at $V=-50$ (the bank owes money) and forgot that the 55 it posted is lost, which more than covers the 50 owed.

options.label: Positive: the lost collateral is larger than the debt

takeaway: Posted collateral that is not returned is a claim on the defaulter: over-posting can create exposure even when the trades are out of the money.

setup: A trader is long a one-year forward on 10,000 bags of coffee at USD 500 per bag (notional USD 5m, zero value today). Annual price volatility is 25%, zero-mean normal, 252 trading days a year. Collateral is called once exposure exceeds USD 500,000 and arrives after a 2-day remargining period; the agreement is fully enforced. One-sided 95% $z = 1.645$.
ask: The 95% maximum credit exposure is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 16,000
options.why: Two slips: used $2/252$ instead of its square root, and left out the USD 500,000 threshold.

options.label: ≈ USD 183,000
options.why: Counted only the 2-day move and forgot that exposure can sit at the USD 500,000 threshold before the margin call.

options.label: ≈ USD 2,060,000
options.why: Used the full one-year volatility for the move instead of the 2-day remargining period.

takeaway: With full margining, exposure peaks at threshold plus the move during the remargining period, not the move over the life.

setup: Best-case benefit of variation-margin collateral on a 3-year portfolio, margin period of risk 23 days, 250 trading days a year. Rule of thumb: uncollateralized EPE $\approx 0.5\sqrt{T/\text{MPoR}}$ times collateralized EPE, with $T$ and MPoR in the same unit. The reduction is then $1 - 1/\text{ratio}$.
ask: Before the reduction, the ratio of uncollateralized to collateralized EPE is closest to:

options.why: Left $T$ in years (3) against MPoR in days (23) instead of putting both in days.
Computed $1/\text{ratio}$, the collateralized-to-uncollateralized figure, instead of the ratio itself.
Dropped the factor 0.5 and used $\sqrt{T/\text{MPoR}}$ alone.

takeaway: Express $T$ and MPoR in the same unit; a ratio near 3 means collateral can remove roughly two thirds of the exposure at best.

setup: A cash-collateralized exposure has annual volatility 15.0% (zero-mean normal). The remargin period, worst-case delays included, is 30 days; assume 250 days a year. $\text{PFE} = z_\alpha\,\sigma\sqrt{T_M}$ with $z_{99\%} = 2.33$ and $T_M$ in years.
ask: The 99% PFE at the end of the 30 days is closest to:

options.why: Used variance ($0.15^2 = 0.0225$) instead of volatility and also skipped the square root of time.
Skipped the square root: multiplied by $T_M = 0.12$ instead of $\sqrt{0.12}$.
Applied no time scaling at all: $2.33 \times 15\%$ is the one-year PFE.

takeaway: PFE scales with $\sqrt{T}$: 30 days is about a third of a year's volatility, so roughly 12% against 35% for a full year.

setup: Over a 10-day remargining period a position's change in value is zero-mean normal. Annual volatility is 10% with 252 trading days, so the 10-day standard deviation is $\sigma_T = 10\% \times \sqrt{10/252} \approx 1.99\%$. The 99% PFE uses $z = 2.33$. Expected exposure is $E[\max(X,0)]$.
ask: Compared with $\sigma_T$, the expected exposure over the period is:

options.label: About one standard deviation, near 2.0%
options.why: Reported $\sigma_T$ itself as EE; $E[\max(X,0)]$ is only the positive half of the distribution, about $0.4\,\sigma_T$.

options.label: More than two standard deviations, near 4.6%
options.why: Quoted the 99% PFE ($2.33\,\sigma_T$), which is a tail quantile, not the average exposure.

takeaway: EE is a mean of positive outcomes only: for a zero-mean normal it is about 40% of $\sigma_T$, and the confidence level plays no part.

setup: A swap has a constant expected positive exposure of 5% of notional and the counterparty's credit spread is 300 bps a year. Ignore wrong-way risk and use the quick approximation: running-spread CVA $\approx$ EPE $\times$ credit spread.
ask: The size of the CVA charge as a running spread is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 1.5 bps
options.why: Decimal slip: read $0.05 \times 300 = 15$ bps as 0.15 and cut it a further tenfold.

options.label: ≈ 60 bps
options.why: Divided instead of multiplied: $300/5 = 60$.

options.label: ≈ 1,500 bps
options.why: Put EPE in as 5 rather than 0.05 (percent used as a whole number).

takeaway: A small percentage times a spread in bps shrinks the number: 5% of 300 bps is 15 bps, not 1,500.

setup: Unilateral CVA as a spread, $\approx -\text{EPE} \times s$, on a swap with a counterparty bank. Data: 1-year risk-neutral default probability 6.5%; continuously compounded risk-free rate 2.6%; yield on the counterparty's credit instrument underlying the swap 5.8%; loss given default 75%; average EPE 5.0%, constant.
ask: Which figure is the credit spread $s$ that enters the formula?

options.label: 2.4%: the 3.2% spread scaled by the 75% LGD
options.why: Applied LGD a second time; the spread already embeds both default probability and loss given default.

options.label: 3.2%: the yield less the risk-free rate
5.8%: the yield itself
options.why: Took the full yield, which still contains the risk-free rate; a spread is the excess over risk-free.

options.label: 6.5%: the default probability
options.why: Used a probability as if it were a spread; PD is already built into the spread.

takeaway: The spread is yield minus risk-free; PD and LGD are not multiplied in again.

setup: Strongcore bought a 3-year at-the-money European call from a risky counterparty: $S = K = $ USD 25.0m, volatility 20%, risk-free 3% continuous, $N(d_1) = 0.6675$, $N(d_2) = 0.5345$. The counterparty has a constant 6% hazard rate and 30% recovery. CVA $\approx \text{LGD} \times \text{PD}(0,T) \times V$, where $V$ is the option's current value.
ask: First step: the option value $V$ is closest to:

options.label: USD 3.3m
options.why: Forgot to discount the strike: $25 \times (0.6675 - 0.5345)$.

options.label: USD 12.2m
options.why: Kept only the discounted strike leg $Ke^{-rT}N(d_2)$.

options.label: USD 16.7m
options.why: Kept only the first leg $S\,N(d_1)$ and never subtracted the strike leg.

takeaway: Value the claim first: a call worth USD 4.5m, not S N(d1) alone, is the exposure that default can take away.

setup: CityBank holds a 5-year European put: $S = 70$, $K = 50$, volatility 30%, risk-free 4% continuous, $N(d_1) = 0.870$, $N(d_2) = 0.680$. Treat the present-valued expected exposure as the put's value. The counterparty's default probability over 5 years is 8% and LGD is 75%. CVA $\approx \text{LGD} \times \text{PD} \times V$.
ask: The CVA deducted from the put is closest to:

options.why: Multiplied LGD by PD only ($0.75 \times 0.08$) and never applied it to the put's value.
Used only the strike leg $Ke^{-rT}N(-d_2) \approx 13.1$ as the exposure.
Dropped the default probability: $0.75 \times 4.0$.

takeaway: CVA is a small slice of the exposure: LGD times a modest PD times V (here 6% of 4.0), not the exposure itself.

setup: A 3-year exposure with no netting, collateral or wrong-way risk. Expected exposure is USD 32m in each of years 1, 2 and 3. The default hazard rate is a constant 10% a year, but recovery falls 90%, 80%, 70%, so LGD is 10%, 20%, 30%. Risk-free rate 4% continuous, discounting at each year-end. Each year's CVA term is LGD $\times$ DF $\times$ EE $\times$ marginal PD.
ask: Which year contributes the largest term to the CVA?

options.label: Year 1, the year with the highest marginal default probability
options.why: Marginal PD is highest in year 1 (9.5%), but LGD is only 10% there; the product is smallest.

options.label: Year 2, the middle year
options.why: Neither trend peaks in the middle: LGD rises 10% to 30% faster than marginal PD falls (9.5% to 7.8%), so the product keeps rising.

options.label: Year 3, the year with the highest LGD

takeaway: Watch every moving part: LGD tripling beats the fall in marginal PD and discounting, so the last year dominates.

setup: One-year horizon. Discounted expected exposure is AUD 48m in each direction. Default probabilities: institution 3.3%, counterparty 1.5%; recoveries: institution 75%, counterparty 90%. UCVA $= -48\text{m} \times \text{LGD}_C \times \text{PD}_C$. BCVA = CVA + DVA, each leg multiplied by the other party's survival probability, defaults independent.
ask: Switching from UCVA to BCVA changes the institution's reported value by about:

options.label: ≈ AUD 2,400
options.why: Applied only the survival adjustment to the CVA leg and left out the DVA leg altogether.

options.label: ≈ AUD 72,000
options.why: Took the size of the UCVA charge itself as the change.

options.label: ≈ AUD 1,170,000
options.why: Used the 75% recovery rate as LGD in the DVA leg instead of 25%.

takeaway: Moving to BCVA adds the own-default benefit (DVA) and trims the CVA charge slightly, so value rises by about 5 times the UCVA charge here.

setup: Bilateral CVA for Bank Gamma against Bank Phi, first-to-default adjusted with independent defaults. Gamma's discounted exposure to Phi is CNY 60m and Phi's exposure to Gamma is CNY 45m. Annual PD: Gamma 2.5%, Phi 1.8%. Recovery: Gamma 82%, Phi 92%. Convention: BCVA = CVA + DVA, CVA negative, DVA positive.
ask: From Gamma's perspective the BCVA is:

options.label: A net charge: negative, because Gamma's exposure (60) is larger
options.why: Compared exposures only; Gamma's 18% LGD against Phi's 8% and its higher PD make the DVA leg far larger than the CVA leg.

options.label: A net benefit: positive, because the DVA leg is larger

takeaway: Do not rank the legs by exposure alone: the weaker credit (higher PD and LGD) earns a larger DVA, so BCVA can be a gain.

setup: From CityBank's view, a swap with FinCorp has EPE 6.00% and ENE $-4.20\%$ (entered negative); the maximum PFE is 18.0%. CityBank's own credit spread is 110 bps and FinCorp's is 250 bps. BCVA $= -\text{EPE} \times s_C - \text{ENE} \times s_P$, with $s_C$ the counterparty's spread and $s_P$ the firm's own.
ask: The DVA term, $-\text{ENE} \times s_P$, is closest to:

options.label: −4.6 bps
options.why: Dropped the minus sign on ENE: the negative ENE turns the DVA term into a gain.

options.label: +10.5 bps
options.why: Multiplied ENE by FinCorp's 250 bps instead of CityBank's own 110 bps.

takeaway: DVA uses your own spread and the negative-exposure side; the maximum PFE never enters the quick formula.

setup: An interest rate swap has a risky duration (risky annuity) of 4 years. Its upfront CVA is 1% of notional. Convert the upfront charge into a running spread.
ask: The CVA as a running spread is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 2.5 bps
options.why: Decimal slip: treated 1% as 10 bps before dividing by 4.

options.label: ≈ 100 bps
options.why: Left out the duration: 1% is 100 bps as an upfront figure, not a spread per year.

options.label: ≈ 400 bps
options.why: Multiplied by the duration instead of dividing: $100 \times 4$.

takeaway: Running spread = upfront / risky annuity: spreading the cost over 4 years of expected premiums makes it smaller.

setup: A netting set holds an IRS (marginal CVA $-1.450$) and a cross-currency swap (marginal CVA $-1.550$). The CCS is executed first with incremental CVA $-2.100$; the IRS is executed second. Incremental CVAs taken in order of execution add up to the netted total, which equals the sum of the marginal CVAs.
ask: The IRS's incremental CVA, compared with its marginal CVA of $-1.450$, is:

options.label: Equal, $-1.450$
options.why: Treated incremental as marginal; but the first trade already took $-2.100$, so the second gets only what is left of the $-3.000$ total.

options.label: Larger in size, about $-5.100$
options.why: Added the total $-3.000$ and the first trade's $-2.100$ instead of subtracting it.

takeaway: Incrementals are order-dependent but must still sum to the total: the first trade takes its standalone CVA and the second gets the remainder.
